Nescio qua natale solum dulcedine cunctos / ducit et immemores non sinit esse sui — the couplet translated in the text.

english.html: And setting out the facts still more fully, he deduced that, having remained seven or eight years in the King's service in the wars, and some months in Spain to see the country, being desirous of seeing again his kinsfolk, his native land, Sanxi his child, and still more the said de Rols his wife, he had, three years ago and more, returned to the said place of Artigat.

These three goads here were in truth very sharp ones, to bring a man back from a distant country: namely, the sweetness of one's native land, the tender love of one's children, and the love of one's wife. For as to one's native land, one could scarcely express (says Cicero in some place) what sweetness, what pleasure, what love and delight it contains <sup class="mk" data-key="a">a</sup>; which, being infinitely great, brings it about that another country, though it be more beautiful, pleasant and fertile, will nevertheless never be found so gracious or so delectable <sup class="mk" data-key="b2">b2</sup>. Witness Ulysses, who of old dared well to prefer Ithaca (where he was born), stony, set like a little nest among the rough rocks and almost inaccessible, to the immortality that Calypso the nymph had offered him <sup class="mk" data-key="c2">c2</sup>. On which subject Ovid says <sup class="mk" data-key="q">q</sup>,

notes.citation: Cicero, Post reditum ad Quirites (section not located)
notes.original: Ciceron en l'oraiſon qu'il eut ad Quiri tes poſt reditũ.
notes.gloss: Cicero's speech to the people on his return from exile, on the sweetness of one's native land.

notes.citation: Digest 31 (De legatis et fideicommissis II), l. Qui habebat (fragment not identified); Accursius on Code 4.55 (Si servus exportandus veneat), the last law
notes.original: l. qui habebat. D. de leg. ij. Accurſe en la l. finale. C. ſi ſeru. expor. ven.
notes.gloss: Cited for the sweetness of one's own country over any other; the bearing of the two passages has not been verified.

notes.original: Homere au v. de l'Odiſ ſee. Cicerõ au. j. de Oratore.
notes.gloss: Cicero: the wisest of men preferred Ithaca, "fixed like a little nest upon the roughest of rocks," to immortality — the words Coras paraphrases.

english.html: By I know not what sweetness the native soil draws all men, and does not suffer them to be unmindful of it.
